turns.user: Quick one for a trip in late November. I'm booking Boston (BOS) to Lisbon (LIS) through Frankfurt on a single itinerary, and I'd like to know whether one ticket means the airline has to rebook me if the first leg is delayed and I miss the connection. I've read conflicting things on forums, so a clear answer would help.
turns.assistant:
Yes, in most cases a single ticket with one booking reference (one PNR) protects you. If the first flight is late and you miss the Frankfurt connection because of that delay, the airline is responsible for rebooking you on the next available option to Lisbon, usually at no extra charge.

A few things to check before you pay:

- Make sure both legs are on the same ticket. Two separate bookings, even on the same day, give you no protection. If the first leg is cancelled, you'd be dealing with two different carriers.
- Look at the connection time. Frankfurt is large and connections under about 60 minutes can be tight, especially if you change terminals or need to clear passport control. Around 90 minutes is much safer.
- Check whether the second leg is operated by a partner airline. Rebooking is easier when both legs are on one carrier or alliance partners that share the booking.
- Keep the delay paperwork. If the first flight arrives more than three hours late, you may also be owed compensation under EU261, depending on the route and the carrier.

If you tell me the carrier and the connection time, I can help you judge how tight it is.

turns.user: how do i solve this one: a 5 kg block slides down a 30 degree incline with mu = 0.2. need the acceleration. i always get lost on the free body diagram part so i never get to the actual math
turns.assistant:
Start with the free body diagram and the math mostly falls out.

1. Draw the block as a dot and show three forces: gravity mg pointing straight down, the normal force N perpendicular to the surface, and kinetic friction f pointing up the incline, opposite the motion.
2. Tilt your axes. Use x along the incline (positive down the slope) and y perpendicular to it. This is the step that saves you. Gravity has to be split into components: mg sin(30°) along the slope and mg cos(30°) into the surface.
3. Y-direction: nothing accelerates perpendicular to the surface, so N = mg cos(30°).
4. X-direction: net force = ma gives mg sin(30°) - μN = ma. Substitute N: ma = mg sin θ - μ mg cos θ.
5. Mass cancels, so a = g(sin θ - μ cos θ) = 9.8(0.5 - 0.2 × 0.866) ≈ 3.2 m/s² down the slope.

The mass doesn't matter at all here, which surprises most people the first time.

turns.user: ok got 3.2. that makes sense. how would i do it if the block is going UP the incline instead, same numbers
turns.assistant:
Going up, friction flips direction, so it points down the slope and adds to gravity's pull back.

1. Forces along the slope: the gravity component mg sin θ pulls down the incline, and friction μN also points down the incline.
2. The normal force doesn't change: N = mg cos θ.
3. Net force along the slope: -mg sin θ - μ mg cos θ = ma, using 'up the slope is positive' as your convention.
4. Mass cancels again: a = -g(sin θ + μ cos θ) = -9.8(0.5 + 0.173) ≈ -6.6 m/s².

The negative sign means it's slowing down while it moves up, at about 6.6 m/s². If the problem asks how far it goes before stopping, use v² = u² + 2as with the starting speed u and a = -6.6 m/s².

turns.user: why does the derivative of x^2 come out to 2x?? i can do the power rule no problem but i dont actually get WHY it works. feels like magic and i hate that
turns.assistant:
The derivative is the slope of the curve at a point, and you can find that slope directly.

Take a point x and a tiny step h to the right, at x + h. The slope of the line between the two points on the curve is rise over run:

[(x + h)² − x²] / h

Expand the top: (x + h)² = x² + 2xh + h², so the numerator is 2xh + h². Divide by h and you get 2x + h.

Now shrink the step. As h gets closer to 0, the secant line turns into the tangent line and the slope becomes 2x + 0 = 2x. That's the limit definition of the derivative. The power rule is a shortcut for doing this expansion in general.

Think of it as: how much does x² change when x changes a tiny bit? Near x = 3, a small nudge in x changes x² by about 6 times that nudge. The 6 is 2x.

turns.user: ok the limit thing works for x^2. but how does it generalize to x^3, i dont wanna just memorize 3x^2 as a rule without knowing where it comes from
turns.assistant:
Same process, just a bigger expansion. Use the binomial theorem:

(x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³

Subtract x³ and divide by h:

[(x + h)³ − x³] / h = 3x² + 3xh + h²

As h goes to 0, every term with h in it vanishes and you're left with 3x².

The general pattern for xⁿ: when you expand (x + h)ⁿ, the term that survives after dividing by h is the one where you pick h from exactly one of the n factors. There are n ways to choose which factor gives the h, and each leaves x^(n−1). So the derivative is n·x^(n−1).

If you want a sanity check, look at x³ at x = 2. The slope should be 3·4 = 12. Moving x from 2 to 2.001 changes x³ from 8 to about 8.012, which is roughly 12 times the nudge.

turns.user: ok so im trying to decide how to make bread in my dorm kitchen. three options i keep going back and forth on: sourdough starter (heard it tastes way better but you have to feed it), instant yeast (i bought a packet already), or the active dry yeast thats in my cupboard. which is least hassle and still tastes decent. be honest
turns.assistant:
For a dorm kitchen, instant yeast is the best balance of effort and taste.

Sourdough starter gives the best flavor, but it needs feeding every day or so if it's sitting on the counter, or weekly if you keep it in the fridge. It also takes roughly a week or more to build a starter that's strong enough to bake with. If you only bake now and then, it'll sit neglected and die, which is a waste of the effort.

Instant and active dry yeast are both fine. Instant is more consistent: it goes straight into the flour, works faster, and rises more predictably. Active dry needs to be dissolved in warm water first, and it's a bit slower. Flavor between the two is close enough that you won't notice in a basic loaf.

So: instant yeast for now. Your active dry yeast works too if you want to use what's already in the cupboard. Save the sourdough for when you know you'll bake every week.

turns.user: ok so if i go instant do i still need to proof it first or just dump it in with the flour. also my dorm kitchen is kinda cold, does that matter
turns.assistant:
Dump it in with the flour. Instant yeast is designed to be mixed straight into the dry ingredients, so you don't need to proof it. Whisk it into the flour and salt first so it's evenly spread, then add the water.

A cold kitchen matters a lot. Yeast works slowly below about 20°C (68°F), so the first rise could take two to three hours instead of one. A few tricks:

- Use water around 35 to 38°C (warm to the touch, not hot). Hot water above about 50°C will kill the yeast.
- Put the dough in the microwave with a mug of boiling water next to it. Keep the door closed and the microwave off.
- Set it on top of the fridge, which is often warmer than the rest of the kitchen.

Judge the rise by the dough roughly doubling in size, not by the clock.

turns.user: I'm a working parent so I only get about 45 min a day for side projects. I've got a feature branch that's been open for three weeks and main has moved a lot since. Priya has also pushed a couple commits to my branch. Should I rebase my branch onto main or merge main into my branch? I don't want to make things worse.
turns.assistant:
Merge main into your branch, because Priya is pushing to it too.

Rebasing rewrites commit history. That's fine on a branch only you use, but once someone else has pulled it, a rebase means they have to reset or cherry-pick their local copy, which causes confusion and sometimes lost commits. Since she's already pushed to it, rebasing is the riskier choice.

With a merge:

1. git checkout feature/your-branch
2. git pull (this gets Priya's latest commits)
3. git merge origin/main
4. Resolve any conflicts, then git commit and git push

Your history will have a merge commit in it, which looks messy but is harmless. You can tidy it up at the end when the PR is ready.

turns.user: ok merge then. but i want the PR history to be clean for review. is squash merge at the end the fix for that or do i need to rebase at some point anyway
turns.assistant:
Squash merge is the usual answer, and you don't need to rebase at all.

When you squash merge a PR, GitHub combines every commit from the branch into one commit on main. The merge commits and 'fix typo' commits disappear from main's history. While the PR is open, reviewers still see the individual commits, which is what they look at.

Two things to watch:

- Priya's commits get squashed too, so check that she's fine with that and that the squashed commit message credits her if your team cares about that.
- After a squash merge, the branch no longer shares history with main. If you keep working on the same branch afterwards, you'll get conflicts later. Delete the branch and start a new one from main for the next piece of work.

So: merge main while you're reviewing, squash on merge, and you're done.
